title: Indic Reasoning and Debating — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): Components of Cognition
*Understand the structure and functions of cognition.
*Explore and describe the different levels and aspects of thinking.
Types of Cognition and Its Validity
*Identify and differentiate various types of cognition.
*Learn and apply processes involved in cognition.
*Understand and implement methods for validating cognition.
Elements of Reasoning
*Comprehend the fundamental processes and concepts in reasoning.
*Analyze the steps our minds take in connecting ideas and drawing conclusions.
Definition Making
*Master the art of defining concepts clearly and precisely.
*Use definitions to enhance clarity and strength in communication and argumentation.
Debating Techniques
*Understand the role and structure of argumentation in debating.
*Learn and apply various debating techniques.
Error Detection
*Develop skills to identify logical fallacies and errors in arguments.
*Enhance the ability to critically analyze and refine reasoning in debates.
*Application of Reasoning and Debating Concepts
*Apply reasoning and debating skills to real-life scenarios.
*Develop the competence to analyze, critique, and counter misleading information in various contexts.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course, the student will gain -
Develop the capability to understand the Bharatiya Knowledge landscape
Develop the art of reasoning and argumentation
Develop rational thinking
Develop the skill of debating based on the rigorous Indic method of Vada.
Explain and demonstrate the classical Indian intellectual culture of inquiry.

title: Bridging Tradition and Technology through AI Enhanced Mudras — Curriculum
content:
General Information about the curriculum: The course "Bridging Tradition and Technology: AI-Enabled Mudras" is conceptualized as the first step of a systematic program that synthesizes the wisdom of Indian traditions and the power of modern technology. The course introduces students to the world of mudras—Indian cultural, spiritual, and artistic traditions of hand gestures—and their increasing usefulness in fields such as artificial intelligence and gesture recognition. This grounding phase is designed to provide students with a general but detailed overview of mudras in historical, cultural, well-being, and performative situations. Alongside these conventional guidelines, the course provides introductory knowledge about AI and machine learning, taking into account their impact on gesture analysis, recognition, and creative synthesis with dance, wellness, and communication. Being a foundation module, the course lays the foundation which subsequent-level modules can construct upon. Through encouraging students to think of mudras both as cultural artifacts and living practice which can be substantively fleshed out by technology, the course ties tradition and innovation together and equips learners to react critically and creatively to both traditional knowledge structures and innovative digital technologies.
Program educational Objective(s): Introduce learners to the traditional knowledge systems of Indian Mudras in dance, yoga, and culture.
Explore the scientific, spiritual, and communicative aspects of Mudras.
Provide foundational understanding of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) in gesture recognition.
Enable learners to integrate Mudras with AI-driven tools for education, performance, and wellness applications.
Develop critical and ethical perspectives on technology’s role in preserving and innovating cultural traditions.
Course Outcome: CO1: Explain the origin, meaning, and classification of Indian Mudras.
CO2: Demonstrate practical knowledge of key Mudras in dance, yoga, and healing.
CO3: Analyze the neurological, cultural, and symbolic significance of Mudras.
CO4: Understand and apply basic AI/ML concepts in gesture recognition.
CO5: Design small-scale AI-enhanced Mudra recognition/representation projects.
CO6: Critically evaluate the ethical and cultural implications of technology in traditional practices.

26.0: Activity 1 Student Seminars : Role Play -Roleplay – AI as a Choreographer (Human Computer Interaction) Students form small groups of 4–5 members, where one student acts as the AI and the others act as dancers.
The AI does not invent new moves but gives pattern-based instructions such as repeat a move, mirror it on the opposite side, rotate it by 90° or 180°, or combine two moves into a sequence.
The dancers follow these AI-like instructions to build a short dance sequence together.
After performing, the group reflects on how the AI guided creativity, whether the dance felt original or more like a remix, and how this relates to real AI tools that support choreographers.
Through this activity, students learn that AI usually works by recognizing and applying patterns, while humans provide the creativity and emotional expression.
27.0: Activity 2 In this activity, one student shows pictures of different hand mudras, and the others try to identify and classify them just like an AI system would, then they reflect on which features make recognition easier, such as finger positions, angles, and symmetry.
28.0: Activity 3 In this activity, students form groups and discuss where AI can support the arts such as theater, music, dance, painting, and its healing power, and then each group presents a mini use case based on their ideas.

title: Indic Way of Creative Design Visualization — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This course introduces students to creative design visualization rooted in Indic Knowledge Systems. It aims to help learners explore philosophical, artistic, and practical dimensions of creativity (Pratibha), bridging Indic traditions with modern visualization practices.
Course Outcome: • To understand and apply Indic concepts of Pratibha, Bhavana, and Rasa in exploring creativity as revelation rather than invention, fostering authentic and intuitive design processes.
- To integrate philosophical principles from Yoga, Vedanta, and Vastusutra Upanishad into visualization practices that bridge the inner (subtle) and outer (gross) realms of creative realization.
- To cultivate inner stillness, focus, and awareness through Dharana, Dhyana, and Yoga Nidra, enabling visualization as a meditative and disciplined act of design creation.
- To analyze and apply frameworks such as Rekha Vidya, Koshthaka, and Mandala to interpret geometry, space, and form as expressions of Rta (cosmic order) and sacred harmony.
- To employ Indic creative values such as Aucitya, Viveka, and Loka Dharma in shaping contextually appropriate, culturally rooted, and ethically attuned design outcomes.
- To reimagine nature, ritual, and symbolism as participatory co-creators in the design process, grounding creative expression in Prakriti, Bhava, and Sattva for ecological and emotional balance.
- To practice visualization as Sadhana, harmonizing knowledge (Jnana), action (Karma), and devotion (Bhakti) to transform design into a conscious act of alignment, service, and self-realization.
Curriculum: Unit I: Introduction and Philosophical Foundations of Creativity (1–12)
- Characterizing Creativity (Pratibha) in Indic Knowledge Systems (Modules 01–03).
- Exploring Vedic and Yogic sources that define creativity as sacred revelation rather than invention (Modules 04–09).
- Understanding Pratibha through the lenses of Buddhi Yoga, Sankhya, and Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras (Modules 04–09).
- Examining Nyaya and Vaisheshika systems that ground creativity in epistemic clarity and ontological precision (Modules 10–12).
- Analyzing how cognition, logic, and sacred perception together shape the emergence of creative insight (Modules 10–12).
Unit II:Creativity in Language, Literature, and Arts (13–30)
- Understanding language (Vyakarana) as a creative and cognitive framework that links sound, meaning, and form (Modules 13–15).
- Exploring Sanskrit poetics (Kavya) as a mode of knowledge where rasa and dhvani transform emotion into aesthetic experience (Modules 16–18).
- Analyzing classical literary theorists like Rajaśekhara and Abhinavagupta to understand the principles of aucitya and intuitive expression (Modules 19–23).
- Examining the creative process in the performing arts (Natya) as embodied philosophy and ritual offering (Modules 22–24).
- Investigating how visual arts and architecture express sacred vision through proportion, symbolism, and form (Modules 25–30).
Unit III: Yogic and Meditative Methods of Visualization (31–39)
- Studying Dharana as the discipline of focused visualization that bridges intention, concentration, and manifestation (Modules 31–33).
- Understanding Dhyana as a meditative state where inner stillness reveals authentic form and symbol (Modules 34–36).
- Exploring Yoga Nidra as a structured method of sacred imagination and symbolic emergence (Modules 37–39).
- Applying Yogic and meditative practices to creative design as acts of awareness and alignment with Rta (Modules 31–39).
Unit IV: Techniques and Practices of Indic Visualization (40–48)
- Exploring nature-based design as co-creation with Prakriti, understanding ecological rhythm and symbolic aesthetics (Modules 40–42).
- Studying Rekha Vidya, the Indic science of sacred geometry, to interpret form as vibrational order and cosmic harmony (Modules 43–45).
- Analyzing Indic symbolism and its translation into contemporary creative contexts (Modules 44–45).
- Understanding rituals as immersive and multisensory design frameworks linking intention, participation, and closure (Modules 46–48).
- Applying sacred forms and experiential principles to develop emotionally resonant and ethically grounded design (Modules 40–48).
Unit V: Philosophy of Visualization (49–60)
- Exploring the metaphysical journey from Avyakta (unmanifest) to Vyakta (manifest) as the basis of creative realization (Modules 49–51).
- Understanding Mandala and Koshthaka as symbolic and spatial frameworks that encode cosmic order (Modules 50–54).
- Studying Tattva, Shabda, and Antahkarana as metaphysical links between essence, vibration, and form (Modules 55–57).
- Learning the sequential procedure of visualization from conceptualization to consecration as outlined in the Vastusutra Upanishad (Modules 58–60).
- Reflecting on visualization as Sadhana that integrates knowledge, ethics, and art into a unified creative discipline (Modules 49–60).

title: Indic Design Thinking — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This course introduces students to Design Thinking through the lens of Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS). It aims to equip learners with critical, creative, and ethical approaches to problem-solving, bridging traditional Indic concepts with modern design methodologies.
Course Outcome: • To integrate Indic philosophical principles such as Atma Bodha, Viveka, and Dharma with modern design thinking frameworks to create ethical and human-centered innovations.
- To cultivate empathy, self-awareness, and contextual sensitivity through Indic practices like Samvada, Svadhyaya, and Ahimsa for socially responsible design solutions.
- To apply Indic creativity concepts such as Pratibha, Lila, and Vikalpanam in generating multiple, sustainable, and culturally rooted design ideas.
- To evaluate and refine design outcomes using Indic frameworks like Saptapadi, Chikitsa, and Sarva-Bhuta Hita, ensuring holistic well-being and long-term impact.
- To practice design as Sadhana,an inner discipline that harmonizes reflective practice, ethical awareness, and continuous improvement in professional and academic contexts.
Curriculum: Unit I: Foundations of Design Thinking (1-16)
- Understanding Design Thinking: Explore conceptual foundations, stages, and global relevance of Design Thinking (Modules 01–03).
- Atma Bodha / Svadhyaya (Understanding Self): Learn reflective practices from IKS to integrate self-awareness, ethics, and resilience into the design mindset (Modules 04–07).
- Sandharbha (Context) and Lok Dharma: Study context-mapping and dharmic responsibility in framing design problems (Modules 08–10).
- Samvaada (Dialogue): Engage in dialogic and ethical conversations as design practice (Modules 11–13).
- Sadhana (Dedicated Practice): Cultivate design as inner discipline, integrating mindfulness, resilience, and transformation through practice (Modules 14–16).
Unit II: Empathy and Defining the Design Brief (17-31)
- The Importance of Empathy: Apply empathy and Indic ethics like Ahimsa in research and mapping user needs (Modules 17–19).
- Personas and Journey Maps: Develop holistic user personas and journey maps enriched with IKS concepts like saṃskāras, bhāvas, and lok dharma (Modules 20–22).
- Viveka (Discerning Intelligence): Use discernment to diagnose root causes and ethically frame problems (Modules 23–25).
- Samasya Lakshanam (Problem Identification): Apply problem characterization and root cause analysis with Indic sensitivity (Modules 26–28).
- Framing the Design Challenge: Craft clear, context-sensitive problem statements and POVs guided by IKS principles (Modules 29–31).
Unit III: Generating ideas and testing (32-46)
- Pratibha (Creative Intelligence): Integrate maker’s and experiencer’s intelligence with mindfulness and IKS creativity practices (Modules 32–34).
- Intuition and Inspiration (Pratyabhijña): Harness intuition, recognition, and playfulness (Līlā) to enrich ideation (Modules 35–37).
- Vikalpanam (Generating Options): Generate multiple possibilities and elegant, non-harming solutions aligned with dharma (Modules 38–40).
- Modern Creativity Techniques: Explore brainstorming, visual thinking, SCAMPER, and TRIZ while aligning with IKS values (Modules 41–43).
- Evaluating Ideas: Use discernment, Saptapadi, MoSCoW, and IKS ethics to refine and prioritize ideas responsibly (Modules 44–46).
Unit IV: Prototyping and Testing (47-52)
- Building Prototypes: Apply low- and high-fidelity prototyping using Indic principles like roopam–pratiroopam, tala-māna, and rasa (Modules 47–49).
- Testing Prototypes: Conduct reflective and ethical prototype testing through dharma, ahimsa, seva, and pramāṇa frameworks (Modules 50–52).
Unit V: Iteration and Holistic Design (53-60)

title: Indian Knowledge Ecosystem — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course, which means this is a common prerequisite for any course in Indic knowledge studies.
Course Outcome: • To bridge traditional Indic concepts with modern fields like knowledge management and liberal arts, enabling their application in today’s academic and professional contexts.
- To equip students to access and interpret Indic sources for application in modern research, promoting innovative solutions to contemporary challenges.
- To explore the scientific and technological principles within Indic traditions, applying them to contemporary fields like environmental science, linguistics, Design etc.
- To conduct comparative analysis between Indic and modern knowledge systems to inspire new models in education, ethics, and governance.
Curriculum: Unit I: Foundations and Applications of Indic Knowledge (1- 12)
- Concepts of Knowledge: Explore key traditional concepts of knowledge and their evolution in contemporary contexts. Understand the shift from ancient ideas to modern terms like 'knowledge,' 'skills,' and 'education,' and their relevance today.
- Sources of Knowledge: Study the primary sources of Indic knowledge, including oral traditions, manuscripts, and written texts. Learn how these sources contribute to both ancient and modern knowledge systems.
- Vedic Texts and Their Interpretations: Analyze the structure and classification of ancient texts, discussing their role as repositories of knowledge. Compare traditional and modern interpretations, focusing on how these texts continue to influence contemporary thought.
- Knowledge in Rituals: Examine the relationship between knowledge and rituals, particularly the mutual influence between ancient texts and ritual practices.
Unit II: Foundations and Contemporary Relevance of Indic Auxiliary Sciences ( 13- 19)
- Overview of Auxiliary Sciences: Study the traditional sciences that supported ancient knowledge systems, focusing on their original roles and their modern relevance.
- Phonetics and Linguistics: Explore the development of phonetics, phonology, and linguistic principles that have influenced modern language studies.
- Mathematics and Metrics: Analyze the ancient methods of protecting oral texts and prosody, and how these have contributed to the development of mathematics, including binary calculations and the concept of zero.
- Semantics and Hermeneutics: Investigate the protection and interpretation of meanings in ancient texts, leading to foundational ideas in modern semantics and linguistic theory.
- Rituals and Geometry: Understand the procedures and mathematical concepts that were central to ancient rituals, and how they connect to contemporary geometry and other scientific disciplines.
- Astronomy and Meteorology: Examine the traditional knowledge of space and time, and its contribution to modern fields like astronomy and meteorology.
Unit III: Interpretative Frameworks and Philosophical Systems in Indic Knowledge ( 20 -31)
- Interpretation of Ancient Texts: Explore traditional methods of interpreting ancient texts and their modern relevance in areas such as linguistic analysis, cognitive studies, and knowledge management.

title: Indian Knowledge Ecosystem — Curriculum

It explores the foundational principles and philosophical underpinnings that define these classifications. Designed specifically for undergraduate students, this course aims to address both their current academic requirements and future professional needs. Each module within the curriculum is meticulously developed to ensure a deep understanding of the diverse and rich landscape of Indian knowledge traditions. Extensive research has been undertaken to craft a curriculum that is both essential and relevant for students, facilitating a thorough grasp of the subject matter.

Course Highlights: This course focuses on the communication theories and linguistic principles found in Patañjali’s Mahābhāṣya, Vakyapadiya, Bharata Muni's Natya Sastra, etc., the classical texts on Indian grammar, Aestetics and the philosophy of Language. It offers a deep dive into the relationship between language, thought, and meaning while exploring their practical applications in modern communication. The course aims to connect ancient Indian linguistic traditions with contemporary communication frameworks, providing students with a rich interdisciplinary perspective.

title: Indic perspective on Communication and Discourse Analysis — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Course Objectives: ● Understand the foundational principles of communication as explained in various texts such as Mahābhāṣya, etc.,
- Explore the cognitive and structural dimensions of language and speech.

title: Indic perspective on Communication and Discourse Analysis — Curriculum
content:
Unit 1: Foundations – Communication Theory East and West (6 Modules)
Module 1: Defining Communication – Western Models and Indian Perspectives – Introduces what “communication” means (e.g. the Shannon–Weaver transmission model vs. the Sādhāraṇīkaraṇa model from Indian aesthetics)
Module 2: Language, Thought, and Reality – How language shapes thought and reality, comparing Western notions (e.g. Sapir-Whorf hypothesis) with insights from Mahābhāṣya and Vākyapadīya.
Module 3: Speech and Script – Orality in Sanskrit Tradition vs. Modern Media – Primacy of śabda in Indian tradition
Module 4: Communication Ethics – Truth and Purity of Expression – Principles of ethical communication from ancient texts (e.g. “satyam brūyāt, priyam brūyāt” – “speak truth, speak pleasantly”)
Module 5: Communication as Education – The Guru-Śiṣya Dialogue – Communication dynamics in teacher-student interactions
Module 6: Communication Models in Practice – Lasswell to Lokavāda – Canonical Western model (Lasswell’s “Who says What to Whom in What Channel with What Effect”) alongside an ancient Indian communication scenario. (e.g. edicts)
Unit 2: Language and Grammar as Tools for Clarity
Module 7: Panini and Patanjali – Grammar for Effective Communication – Explore how the Sanskrit grammatical tradition aims to eliminate ambiguity in language. (sādhu vs. asādhu words) and grammatical structure contributing to clarity – a principle equally valued in modern writing and editing
Module 8: Constructing Meaning – Words, Sentences, and Context – How meaning is constructed, comparing Mahābhāṣya’s insights with modern linguistics. word-meaning vs sentence-meaning: e.g. the abhihitānvaya view versus anvitābhidhāna . Individual words matter, but context ultimately ensures understanding – useful for crafting clear sentences and avoiding miscommunication
Module 9: Brevity and Substance – Highlight the communication brilliance of sūtras, which convey maximum meaning in minimum words. Balance of brevity and clarity. 'tight-writing' in journalism
Module 10: Rhetoric and Persuasion – Classical Alankāra and Modern Stylistics – Figures of speech and persuasive devices in classical literature. How metaphors, similes, and analogies were used to influence and engage audiences
Module 11: Argumentation and Debate – Art of debate in ancient India and how it aligns with critical thinking today. Adapting one’s approach based on the opponent and audience (noted even in Caraka Saṃhitā) –early insights into audience analysis and persuasive strategy
Module 12: Case Study – Clarity and Persuasion in an Epic Dialogue – Analyze Yudhiṣṭhira’s answers to the Yakṣa to identify techniques of clear explanation and persuasion. Highlight Communication tactics such as using storytelling, appealing to shared values (dharma), and structuring arguments logically
Unit 3: Traditional Media and Performance as Communication
Module 13: Storytelling for Social Communication – Focus on narrative communication. Imparting lessons through engaging animal stories – modern media practices (edutainment, social message films, and even podcasts that use stories to inform).
Module 14: Drama and Non-Verbal Communication – Nātyaśāstra- Natya as communication medium, combining verbal, visual, and emotional expression. Use of rasa (emotional flavor) theory – how conveying a dominant emotion can create shared feeling in an audience
Module 15: Multilingual Communication in Ancient Theatres – Intercultural and cross-audience communication. Modern communication: using vernacular for mass appeal or code-switching among bilingual speakers to effectively reach different social groups
Module 16: Folk Media and Mass Communication – Traditional Indian folk performances (like katha, Kuttu, Yakshagana, puppet shows, street theatre) function as mass communication tools in pre-modern communities – conveying religion, ethics, and social messages to largely oral audiences.
Module 17: Communicating Values and Morals – Epics and Social Messaging
Module 18: Media Writing – Clarity, Tone, and Audience – This practical module connects ancient emphasis on clarity with modern writing skills
Unit 4: Intercultural Communication – Bridging Cultures and Eras
Module 19: Language and Culture in Communication – Concepts of intercultural communication from modern theory (e.g. high-context vs low-context cultures, Hofstede’s cultural dimensions) and correlate them with India’s own rich cultural-linguistic diversity. It sets a foundation by asking: how does culture affect communication styles?
Module 20: Sanskrit as a Link Language – Ancient Lingua Franca – Discusses how Sanskrit functioned as a pan-Indian scholarly lingua franca for centuries, bridging regional cultures. Historical instances of intercultural exchange: for example, ancient universities (Nalanda, Takshashila) where students from across Asia learned in Sanskrit, or how Sanskrit terms were adopted in Southeast Asian languages via Hindu-Buddhist influence. Early intercultural communication through a shared language and provide a springboard to discuss today’s link languages (like English globally) and issues of linguistic dominance and inclusivity.
Module 21: Cross-Cultural Narratives – How Indian stories and ideas were communicated to other cultures. The spread of Panchatantra fables to Persia and Europe (becoming Kalila wa Dimna, then Aesop’s fables), or the travel of Buddhist sermons from India to East Asia. How messages are transformed to resonate with different cultures – a classical precursor to concepts like translation, localization, and cultural framing in global media today.
Module 22: Communication Etiquette and Customs – Polite and effective communication in Indian tradition vs other cultures. For instance, the Indian concept of sambhāṣaṇa (polite conversation). Highlights how cultural norms influence what is considered a “good” communication style.
Module 23: Conflict and Diplomacy – Strategic communication. Advice on diplomacy and message strategy (e.g. how envoys should communicate, use of spies = intelligence gathering, etc.). Students identify age-old tactics for persuading or negotiating with those of different interests.
Module 24: Media Writing – Writing for a Diverse Audience – Exercise guidelines to draft a piece of media content (such as a short opinion column or a social media post) intended for a culturally diverse audience
Unit 5: Integrating Ancient Wisdom with Modern Skills
Module 25: Convergence of Communication Theories – Summarize and synthesize key theories learned. Modern communication theory (e.g. the Transactional Model of communication) and discuss it alongside an Indian parallel or contrast. Concepts like feedback, noise, context (from modern models) were implicitly understood in traditional contexts – for example, the Sādhāraṇīkaraṇa model emphasizes mutual understanding and context
Module 26: Case Study – Modern Media Through an IKS Lens – Analyze a recent viral communication campaign (such as a public health message during a pandemic) and critique it through both modern media theory and an Indic lens
Module 27: Technology, Language, and Future Communication – Intersection of language technologies and ancient linguistic science. Panini’s formal grammar influences modern computational linguistics and even AI natural language processing (rule-based approach = algorithm)
Module 28: Personal Communication and Mindfulness – Indian philosophical traditions views on mindful communication. Concepts such as right speech (samyak vāk) from the Buddha’s teachings and Patanjali’s prescriptions for restraint in speech. Techniques for active listening and empathetic speaking
Module 29: Dharma of Dialogue – Role of communication in building community and harmony
Module 30: Course Synthesis

title: IKS Perspectives on Law and Jurisprudence — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): * To cultivate an appreciation for the rich tradition of Indian Law and jurisprudence.
* To introduce students to the principles and concepts of law and jurisprudence as viewed through the lens of Bharatiya Shastras namely Vyavahara kanda of Dharma Shastra and Danda niti.
* To enhance students' critical thinking and argumentation skills by examining Tarka Shastra, the traditional Indian method of reasoning and debate.
* To provide a comprehensive understanding of the practical applications of these concepts in contemporary legal contexts.
Course Outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Appreciate the historical and cultural significance of Indian contributions to the field of law and jurisprudence.
2. Understand and articulate the basic concepts of law and jurisprudence from the perspective of Bharatiya Shastras.
3. Apply cognitive processes and reasoning techniques rooted in traditional Indian knowledge to legal analysis and problem-solving.
4. Develop effective debating strategies and techniques based on ancient Indian methods.
Curriculum: Unit I: Introduction to Indian legal traditions (1 to 13)
1. Stage one - Oral Tradition and Administration of Justice
2. Stage two - Transition from oral tradition to written law
3. Stage three - The organization of legal texts into Samhitâs and Dharma Shastras
4. Stage four - The integration of Hindu and Buddhist legal traditions
5. Inscriptions as a fundamental source of history

General Information about the curriculum: This course provides an introductory exploration of concepts related to the field of law and jurisprudence from the perspective of Bharatiya Shastras (the ancient and traditional knowledge systems originated in India). It is designed to give students a foundational understanding of various cognitive processes, types of reasoning, definition-making, debating techniques, and error detection methods, with practical applications in the field of law and jurisprudence.
Program educational Objective(s): * To cultivate an appreciation for the rich tradition of Indian Law and jurisprudence.

* To enhance students' critical thinking and argumentation skills by examining Tarka Shastra, the traditional Indian method of reasoning and debate.
* To provide a comprehensive understanding of the practical applications of these concepts in contemporary legal contexts.

3. Apply cognitive processes and reasoning techniques rooted in traditional Indian knowledge to legal analysis and problem-solving.
4. Develop effective debating strategies and techniques based on ancient Indian methods.

title: Indic Meta Thinking - Knowledge about Knowledge — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): Primary Objectives
1. Foundational Understanding
Establish comprehensive knowledge of Indian philosophical systems, particularly Astika and Nastika traditions
Understand the historical development and contemporary relevance of the fourteen Vidyasthanas (knowledge branches)
Develop familiarity with key concepts in Nyaya-Vaisheshika philosophy, including the seven padarthas (categories of existence)
2. Epistemological Mastery
Master the six pramanas (means of valid knowledge): Pratyaksha (perception), Anumana (inference), Upamana (comparison), Shabda (verbal testimony), Arthapatti (postulation), and Anupalabdhi (non-cognition)
Understand the sophisticated analysis of sensory perception and its relationship with cognition
Explore the nature of extraordinary perception and transcendental knowledge states
3. Logical and Analytical Skills
Develop proficiency in the Pancha-avayava (five-membered syllogism) system of logical reasoning
Learn to identify and analyze various types of logical fallacies (Hetvabhasa)
Apply principles of valid inference (Vyapti) in philosophical and practical contexts
4. Metacognitive Development
Cultivate enhanced self-awareness of cognitive processes and thinking patterns
Understand the distinction between valid (Prama) and invalid (Bhrama) cognition
Develop skills in recognizing and correcting cognitive errors and biases
5. Integration and Application
Bridge traditional Indian epistemology with contemporary cognitive science and philosophy
Apply yogic principles of transcendental perception to modern understanding of consciousness
Synthesize diverse philosophical perspectives into coherent frameworks for analysis
Secondary Objectives
6. Cross-Cultural Philosophical Literacy
Compare and contrast Indian and Western approaches to epistemology and logic
Understand the unique contributions of Indian philosophy to global philosophical discourse
Develop appreciation for diverse cultural approaches to knowledge and reasoning
7. Practical Wisdom
Apply philosophical insights to contemporary challenges in education, research, and personal development
Develop enhanced critical thinking skills applicable across disciplines
Cultivate deeper understanding of the relationship between knowledge, consciousness, and spiritual development
Course Outcome: Upon completion of this program, participants will achieve:
Theoretical Mastery
Comprehensive understanding of Indian philosophical schools, particularly Nyaya-Vaisheshika epistemology
Proficiency in the six pramanas (means of valid knowledge) and their applications
Knowledge of advanced concepts including yogic perception and transcendental cognition
Analytical Skills
Mastery of traditional Indian logical structures, including the five-membered syllogism
Ability to identify and analyze logical fallacies (Hetvabhasa) and reasoning errors
Enhanced metacognitive awareness and self-reflective thinking capabilities
Practical Applications
Integration of ancient wisdom with contemporary approaches to knowledge and consciousness
Improved critical thinking and philosophical argumentation skills
Enhanced capacity for cross-cultural philosophical dialogue and research
Personal Transformation
Deeper understanding of the relationship between knowledge, consciousness, and self-realization
Development of practical wisdom applicable to daily life and decision-making
Greater appreciation for the complementary nature of diverse knowledge traditions
The program offers a transformative educational experience that bridges India's philosophical heritage with contemporary understanding, enriching participants' cognitive capabilities while fostering both intellectual rigor and contemplative wisdom.

At its core, this program investigates metacognition—the awareness and understanding of one's own thought processes—through the lens of classical Indian philosophical schools, particularly the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition. Through rigorous analysis of classical texts and methodologies, participants will develop both theoretical understanding and practical skills in critical thinking, logical reasoning, and philosophical analysis.

title: IKS VI: Indian Mathematics — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is a foundation course in Indian Mathematics. Basic working knowledge in Sanskrit and Mathematics is required.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course students will be able to
know the content of the texts in Sanskrit in Indian Mathematics
know the rules and work out the examples in various topics in the subject
understand and apply the concepts, principles and contributions of Indian mathematics and
relate the methods and principles to the modern methodologies.
Curriculum: UNIT I (10 modules)
Sub-Unit 1. Introduction to Indian Mathematics (3 modules)
1.1 Importance of Indian Mathematics
1.2 Contents of some important texts in Indian mathematics
1.3 Indian Decimal Place value system and Zero.
Sub-Unit 2. Eight Operations on Numbers.(4 modules)
2.1. Three Saṅkhyā systems in Sanskrit.
2.2. Operations on Natural Numbers
2.3. Operations on Fractions.
2.4. Operations on Zero.
Sub-Unit 3. Pāṭīgaṇitam – Arithmetic (3 modules)
3.1. Reverse Process, Finding unknown.
3.2. Rule of Three, Inverse Proportion, Rule of Five etc.
3.3. Rule of Barter, Simple Interest.
UNIT II (10 modules)

4.2. Aṅkapāśa-Combinatorics part 1
4.3. Combinatorics part 2

5.1. Śulbasūtras, introduction.
5.2. Śulba constructions.
5.3.Śulba Transformations.
Sub-Unit.6. Kṣetragaṇita –Geometry (4 modules)
6.1. Results and examples on Triangles.
6.2. Interesting examples under Śulba theorem
6.3. Results and examples on Quadrilaterals.
6.4. Results and examples on Circles.
UNIT III (12 modules)
Sub-Unit 7. Algebra (3 modules)
7.1. Operations on Integers, surds
7.2. Algebraic expressions. Equations : Ekavarṇa
7.3. Equations - Anekavarṇa, Bhāvita, Quadratic
Sub-Unit 8. Kuṭṭaka- Indeterminate Equations of degree one (3 modules)
8.1. Methods of Āryabhaṭa I and Bhāskara II
8.2. Varieties of Kuṭṭaka
8.3. Applications in Astronomy
Sub-Unit 9. Vargaprakṛti-Indeterminate Equations of degree2 (3 modules)
9.1. Bhāvanā method.
9.2. Solving Equations of type Nx2 ± C = y2.
9.3. Cakravāla Method
Sub-Unit 10. Trigonometry. (3 modules)
10.1. Brief History of Indian Trigonometry.
10.2. Trigonometric Functions and Identities
10.3. Trigonometric series.

title: IKS Perspectives on Sustainability: Water Management — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Course Objectives: Understand the principles of water management and sustainability in ancient India.
Explore the technological innovations and practices related to hydrology in various ancient Indian civilizations.
Analyze the relevance of traditional water management techniques in contemporary sustainability efforts.
Integrate ancient Indian hydrological knowledge into modern water management practices.
Learning Outcomes: By the end of the course, learners will be able to:
Critically examine the hydrological principles and sustainable water practices found in ancient Indian civilizations using archaeological and textual sources.
Evaluate the philosophical, technological, and ecological dimensions of traditional water management systems and their relevance to current sustainability challenges.
Integrate interdisciplinary insights from history, engineering, environmental science, and culture to propose informed applications of ancient water knowledge in modern contexts.
Tentative Course Plan | Script | PPT | FA | Raw Video
Module 1: Introduction to Hydrology in Ancient India
Overview of the importance of water management in ancient Indian society.
Introduction to key texts and archaeological evidence related to water management.
Comparative analysis of ancient Indian and global hydrological practices.
Module 2: Philosophical Foundations of Water Management in IKS
Role of water in Vedic and post-Vedic literature.
Concepts of natural resource management in Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra.
Water as a sacred element: Cultural and spiritual dimensions.
Module 3: Hydrological Cycle in Ancient Indian Texts
Interpretation of the hydrological cycle in Rigveda, Mahabharata, and Ramayana.
The role of Varaha Mihira and other scholars in systematizing water management.
Understanding the conceptual aspect of hydrological cycle in Indian mythology.
Module 4: Water and Sacred Geography
The role of rivers and water bodies in shaping sacred landscapes.
Pilgrimage sites and the ritual importance of water.
Case studies of sacred rivers like the Ganga, Yamuna, and Sarasvati.
Module 5: Water in Ancient Indian Literature and Arts
Representation of water in ancient Indian literature, including epics and Puranas.
Symbolism of water in Indian arts and architecture.
Influence of water-related themes in temple design and sculpture.
Module 6: Water and Sustainability in Buddhist and Jain Traditions
Water management practices in Buddhist monasteries and Jain communities.
Philosophical approaches to water and sustainability in these traditions.
Integration of water management with spiritual practices.
Module 7: Traditional Water Harvesting Techniques
Overview of traditional water harvesting structures: tanks, wells, and stepwells.
Case studies from Rajasthan, Gujarat, and Tamil Nadu.
Design principles and ecological considerations in traditional structures.
Module 8: Irrigation Systems in the Indus Valley Civilization
Analysis of the irrigation systems at Mohenjo-Daro, Harappa, and Dholavira.
Role of the Indus River in supporting agriculture and urban life.
Sustainable water management practices in the Indus Valley.
Module 9: Water Supply and Urban Planning in Ancient Cities
Water supply systems in ancient cities like Varanasi, Pataliputra, and Ujjain.
Integration of water supply with urban planning.
Comparison with contemporary water supply systems.
Module 10: Flood Management in Ancient India
Understanding flood control mechanisms in ancient India.
Case studies of flood management strategies in the Gangetic Plains.
Philosophical and practical approaches to flood mitigation.
Module 11: Groundwater Management in Ancient India
Techniques for identifying and utilizing groundwater resources.
Use of aquifers and qanats in ancient Indian water systems.
Sustainable practices in groundwater management.
Module 12: Sanitation and Wastewater Management
Examination of sanitation practices in the Indus Valley and later periods.
Historical development of wastewater management technologies.
Environmental and health implications of ancient sanitation practices.
Module 13: Dams and Reservoirs in Ancient India
Examination of the construction and function of ancient dams.
Case studies of Sudarshana Lake and other significant reservoirs.
Engineering principles and long-term sustainability of ancient dams.
Module 14: Legal and Administrative Aspects of Water Management
Water rights and management in ancient Indian legal texts.
Role of the state and local communities in managing water resources.
Conflict resolution and water-sharing practices.
Module 15: Technological Innovations in Ancient Hydrology
Overview of ancient Indian technologies related to water management.
Innovations in canal building, stepwells, and rainwater harvesting.
Transfer of knowledge and its adaptation in different regions.
Module 16: Water and Public Works in Ancient India
Examination of public works related to water management in ancient India.
Role of kings and local rulers in initiating water-related infrastructure.
Case studies of significant public works projects.
Module 17: Impact of Climate on Water Management
Historical impact of climatic changes on water management strategies.
Adaptation to monsoon variability and drought conditions.
Lessons for contemporary water management in the context of climate change.
Module 18: Water Conservation Strategies
Traditional methods of water conservation in different regions.
Role of community participation in water conservation.
Analysis of the effectiveness of ancient water conservation strategies.
Module 19: Historical Development of Water Law in India
Evolution of water laws from ancient to medieval periods.
Role of customary laws and their enforcement.
Comparison with modern water laws and policies.
Module 20: Hydraulic Engineering in Ancient India
Exploration of ancient Indian hydraulic engineering techniques.
Case studies of significant hydraulic structures.
Influence of Indian hydraulic engineering on other civilizations.
Module 21: Case Study: Water Management in the Mauryan Empire
Detailed analysis of water management strategies during the Mauryan period.
Role of state policy in ensuring water security.
Ashoka's contributions to water management.
Module 22: Water Management in the Vijayanagara Empire
Study of water management in the Vijayanagara Empire.
Role of the state and local communities in managing water resources.
Analysis of the impact of water management on the empire's sustainability.
Module 23: Modern Relevance of Ancient Water Management Practices
Exploration of how ancient water management techniques can be applied today.
Case studies of successful modern applications of traditional practices.
Challenges and opportunities in integrating ancient knowledge with modern technology.
Module 24: Water and Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs)
Aligning ancient Indian water management practices with the United Nations SDGs.
Contributions of traditional knowledge to global water sustainability.
Strategies for promoting ancient practices in contemporary water management.
Module 25: Interdisciplinary Approaches to Studying Ancient Hydrology
Integration of archaeology, hydrology, and environmental science.
Use of modern technology to study ancient water management systems.
Collaboration between historians, engineers, and environmental scientists.
Module 26: Comparative Study of Water Management in Different Civilizations
Comparative analysis of water management practices in ancient India, Mesopotamia, Egypt, and China.
Understanding the unique features and shared principles.
Lessons for modern water management from ancient global practices.
Module 27: Study: Visiting/Viewing Documentaries on Ancient Water Management Sites
Understanding significant water management sites in India (e.g., Rani ki Vav, Dholavira, Chand Baori).
Practical analysis of the design, construction, and sustainability of these structures.
Reflection on the experience and its relevance to contemporary water management.
Module 28: Case Study: Public Sanitation in Ancient India
Module 29: Case Study: Reviving Ancient Water Management Practices
Study of one or two instances of the revival of an ancient water management practice in a modern context.
Analysis of the feasibility, benefits, and challenges of implementation in other places.
Module 30: Conclusion and Future Directions
Recap of key learnings from the course.
Discussion on the future of water management in India and the role of IKS.
Reflection on how traditional knowledge can contribute to sustainable water management globally.
Unit Structure
Unit I: Philosophical, Cultural & Textual Foundations of Hydrology in Ancient India
Objective: To understand the cosmological, ethical, and textual foundations of water management in ancient India and relate them to early hydrological insights.
Modules Covered (1-6):
Introduction to Hydrology in Ancient India
Philosophical Foundations of Water Management in IKS

Objective: To explore traditional water harvesting, irrigation, sanitation, engineering, and governance systems and assess their long-term sustainability.

Unit III: Applications, Comparative Perspectives, and Future Integration
Objective: To compare ancient Indian practices with other civilizations and evaluate how traditional water knowledge aligns with modern sustainability frameworks.

content:

NCrF Credit Points

title: Understanding and Appreciating Temple Architecture — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course on Indian Temples and will introduce various dimensions of temples
Course Outcome: At the end of the course the student will gain;
1. Exposure and Awareness: Learners will gain a profound exposure to and awareness of the various dimensions of the temple ecosystem
2. Contemporary Relevance: Learners will understand the temple is the heart of the Indian civilization and will understand the importance of restoring and rejuvenating the temple culture in places it is lost.
3. Intellectual and Aesthetic Enrichment: The course will enrich learners’ intellectual horizons, expanding their understanding and appreciation of the Indian temples.
4. Holistic Perspective: Learners will be inspired to adopt a holistic perspective on the multiple streams of knowledge, various kinds of arts, and the philosophical undercurrent of the temple eco-system
Curriculum: Unit I: Meaning of the Indian Temple
- Etymological definition of the word devālaya
- The Evolution of the concept of Temple from the Vedas, Epics, and the purāṇas
- The concept of a man-made structural temple and the philosophy of a temple
- The entire universe and the human body as a temple
- Streams of knowledge which contribute towards understanding the temple ecosystem
Unit II: Kinds of Temple Architecture
- Rock Cut Architecture and Structural Temples - Hindu, Buddhist, and Jaina
- The Evolution of the concept of Temple from the Vedas, Epics, and the purāṇas
- Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara kinds of architecture
- Overview of the improvisations in temple architecture around the country in various periods of time
- Materials used for temple construction and a brief overview of techniques
Unit III: Structural and Functional Units of a Full-fledged Temple
- The ṣaḍvargas of a temple - details of various parts and their purpose
- Kinds of pillars, windows, ceiling, and architectural ornamentations in a temple
- Function and configuration of the various maṇṭapas, mālikā, and other structural features of a temple
- The difference between the major and minor parts of north Indian and South Indian Temples
Unit IV: Philosophy behind Temple Architecture and Vāstu-puruṣa-maṇḍala
- The concept of the pañca-bhūtas, pañca-kośas, and avasthā-traya represented in the vertical and horizontal planes of the Temple Architecture
- The Story of the vāstu-puruṣa and the making of the maṇḍala
Unit V: Sculptures in Indian Temples
- Representative and Non-representative sculptures
- Discussion of sculptures that represent episodes from the Epics, purāṇas, and folklore; evolution of sculptures across different periods in time and the contribution of different dynasties • Local tastes and flavours in temple sculptures - Temples in India and Greater India (Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand, Bali, and Vietnam)
- Iconography of various deities
- Dance sculptures and their codification
Unit VI: Interpreting Temple inscriptions
- Historical and socio-cultural details that can be derived from temple inscriptions • Various scripts and languages used in temple inscriptions
Unit VII: Multi-faceted functions of a Structural Temple
- Temple as a seat of justice and economic hub
- Temple as a social, spiritual, educational and artistic organisation
Unit VIII: Tīrtha-kṣetra around India
- An overview of the śaiva, vaiṣṇava, and śākta tīrtha-kṣetras around India; their sthala-purāṇas, connection with the Vedic tradition and the Epics
Unit IX: Temple rituals and their meaning; destruction of temples; their rejuvenation in the modern day
- Meaning of various temple rituals; the tradition of the Vedas and the āgamas
o Destruction of temples due to invasions; reconstruction and rejuvenation of temples in the modern day

3. Intellectual and Aesthetic Enrichment: The course will enrich learners’ intellectual horizons, expanding their understanding and appreciation of the Indian temples.
4. Holistic Perspective: Learners will be inspired to adopt a holistic perspective on the multiple streams of knowledge, various kinds of arts, and the philosophical undercurrent of the temple eco-system
Curriculum: Unit I: Meaning of the Indian Temple
- Etymological definition of the word devālaya
- The Evolution of the concept of Temple from the Vedas, Epics, and the purāṇas
- The concept of a man-made structural temple and the philosophy of a temple
- The entire universe and the human body as a temple
- Streams of knowledge which contribute towards understanding the temple ecosystem
Unit II: Kinds of Temple Architecture
- Rock Cut Architecture and Structural Temples - Hindu, Buddhist, and Jaina
- The Evolution of the concept of Temple from the Vedas, Epics, and the purāṇas
- Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara kinds of architecture
- Overview of the improvisations in temple architecture around the country in various periods of time
- Materials used for temple construction and a brief overview of techniques
Unit III: Structural and Functional Units of a Full-fledged Temple
- The ṣaḍvargas of a temple - details of various parts and their purpose
- Kinds of pillars, windows, ceiling, and architectural ornamentations in a temple
- Function and configuration of the various maṇṭapas, mālikā, and other structural features of a temple
- The difference between the major and minor parts of north Indian and South Indian Temples
Unit IV: Philosophy behind Temple Architecture and Vāstu-puruṣa-maṇḍala
- The concept of the pañca-bhūtas, pañca-kośas, and avasthā-traya represented in the vertical and horizontal planes of the Temple Architecture
- The Story of the vāstu-puruṣa and the making of the maṇḍala
Unit V: Sculptures in Indian Temples
- Representative and Non-representative sculptures
- Discussion of sculptures that represent episodes from the Epics, purāṇas, and folklore; evolution of sculptures across different periods in time and the contribution of different dynasties • Local tastes and flavours in temple sculptures - Temples in India and Greater India (Cambodia, Indonesia, Thailand, Bali, and Vietnam)
- Iconography of various deities
- Dance sculptures and their codification
Unit VI: Interpreting Temple inscriptions
- Historical and socio-cultural details that can be derived from temple inscriptions • Various scripts and languages used in temple inscriptions
Unit VII: Multi-faceted functions of a Structural Temple
- Temple as a seat of justice and economic hub
- Temple as a social, spiritual, educational and artistic organisation
Unit VIII: Tīrtha-kṣetra around India
- An overview of the śaiva, vaiṣṇava, and śākta tīrtha-kṣetras around India; their sthala-purāṇas, connection with the Vedic tradition and the Epics
Unit IX: Temple rituals and their meaning; destruction of temples; their rejuvenation in the modern day
- Meaning of various temple rituals; the tradition of the Vedas and the āgamas
o Destruction of temples due to invasions; reconstruction and rejuvenation of temples in the modern day

title: Indian Knowledge Ecosystem — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course, which means this is a common prerequisite for any course in Indic knowledge studies.
Course Outcome: • To bridge traditional Indic concepts with modern fields like knowledge management and liberal arts, enabling their application in today’s academic and professional contexts.
- To equip students to access and interpret Indic sources for application in modern research, promoting innovative solutions to contemporary challenges.
- To explore the scientific and technological principles within Indic traditions, applying them to contemporary fields like environmental science, linguistics, Design etc.
- To conduct comparative analysis between Indic and modern knowledge systems to inspire new models in education, ethics, and governance.
Curriculum: Unit I: Foundations and Applications of Indic Knowledge (1- 12)
- Concepts of Knowledge: Explore key traditional concepts of knowledge and their evolution in contemporary contexts. Understand the shift from ancient ideas to modern terms like 'knowledge,' 'skills,' and 'education,' and their relevance today.
- Sources of Knowledge: Study the primary sources of Indic knowledge, including oral traditions, manuscripts, and written texts. Learn how these sources contribute to both ancient and modern knowledge systems.
- Vedic Texts and Their Interpretations: Analyze the structure and classification of ancient texts, discussing their role as repositories of knowledge. Compare traditional and modern interpretations, focusing on how these texts continue to influence contemporary thought.
- Knowledge in Rituals: Examine the relationship between knowledge and rituals, particularly the mutual influence between ancient texts and ritual practices.
Unit II: Foundations and Contemporary Relevance of Indic Auxiliary Sciences ( 13- 19)
- Overview of Auxiliary Sciences: Study the traditional sciences that supported ancient knowledge systems, focusing on their original roles and their modern relevance.
- Phonetics and Linguistics: Explore the development of phonetics, phonology, and linguistic principles that have influenced modern language studies.
- Mathematics and Metrics: Analyze the ancient methods of protecting oral texts and prosody, and how these have contributed to the development of mathematics, including binary calculations and the concept of zero.
- Semantics and Hermeneutics: Investigate the protection and interpretation of meanings in ancient texts, leading to foundational ideas in modern semantics and linguistic theory.
- Rituals and Geometry: Understand the procedures and mathematical concepts that were central to ancient rituals, and how they connect to contemporary geometry and other scientific disciplines.
- Astronomy and Meteorology: Examine the traditional knowledge of space and time, and its contribution to modern fields like astronomy and meteorology.
Unit III: Interpretative Frameworks and Philosophical Systems in Indic Knowledge ( 20 -31)
- Interpretation of Ancient Texts: Explore traditional methods of interpreting ancient texts and their modern relevance in areas such as linguistic analysis, cognitive studies, and knowledge management.
- Philosophical Systems: Study key philosophical frameworks like Mimaamsaa, Vedaanta, Nyaaya, Vaisheṣika, Saankhya, and Yoga, focusing on their original contexts and their applicability to contemporary issues in philosophy, psychology, and ethics.
- Epic and Narrative Literature: Analyze how ancient epics and other literary works serve as repositories of knowledge, offering direct and indirect insights into various aspects of life, culture, and the environment.
Unit IV: Comprehensive Overview of Indic Knowledge Systems ( 32-40)
- Survey of Key Texts: Study major Indic texts and traditions such as those focused on governance, aesthetics, music, and health, including Arthashaastra, Naatyashaastra, Sangeeta, Alankaarashaastra, Ayurveda, Vaastu, Citra-sutra, Dhanurveda etc.
- Traditional Knowledge Classifications: Examine traditional models of knowledge classification, including:
o The 64 fields of knowledge.
o Three Cleansing Sciences: Ayurveda (body), Yoga (mind), and Vyākaraṇa (speech).
Unit V: Contemporary and Traditional Classifications of Knowledge( 41-55)
- Vedic Knowledge Model
- Health and Wellness: Ayurveda.
- Linguistics: Language studies from Vyaakaraṇa.
- Mathematics: Concepts from Chandas and Sulba-sutras.
- Aesthetics: Principles from Alankaarashaastra.
- Logic: Theories from Nyāya.
- Public Administration: Insights from Arthashaastra.
- Psychology: Ideas from Yoga and Upanishads.
- Ethics: Concepts of Dharma from various texts.
- Research Methods: Investigate the potential for research on traditional knowledge systems using fieldwork, ethnography, and other qualitative methods.

title: SCIENCE IN JAINISM — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course, which means this is a common prerequisite for any course in Jain scientific studies.
Course Outcome: Explain the meaning and essence of Jainism, its focus on self-conquest and spiritual liberation.
Describe the historical evolution of Jainism and the contributions of Mahavira and other Tirthankaras.
Identify and interpret the core ethical principles — Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacharya, and Aparigraha — and apply them to modern life.
Understand Jain metaphysics, including the concepts of Jiva, Ajiva, Karma, and the Six Dravyas.
Analyze the Three Jewels (Ratnatraya) as a holistic path toward self-purification and liberation.
Differentiate between Digambara and Shvetambara traditions, recognizing their philosophical and scriptural distinctions.
Evaluate Jainism’s scientific worldview, including its atomic theory, ecology, and relativity of time.
Relate Jain philosophical concepts such as Anekantavada and Syadvada to modern scientific methods and pluralistic thinking.
Assess the ecological and ethical dimensions of Jainism in the context of sustainability, environmental conservation, and non-violence.
Develop an integrated understanding of how ancient Jain thought aligns with and enriches modern scientific and moral perspectives.
Curriculum: Unit I: Introduction to Jainism (1- 12)
Introduce the fundamental principles of Jainism, including its spiritual, ethical, and philosophical dimensions.
Trace the historical development of Jainism — from its origins and Tirthankaras to its impact on Indian thought and society.
Understand the core doctrines such as Ahimsa, Karma, and Moksha, and their practical applications in daily life.
Explore the scientific and rational aspects of Jain philosophy, including atomic theory, ecology, and relativity concepts.
Analyze the relationship between Jain philosophy and modern scientific thought, emphasizing parallels in cosmology, biology, and ethics.
Develop respect for pluralism and non-violence, fostering inter-religious understanding and sustainable living.
Unit II: Biology in Jainism ( 13- 24)
To explore the Jain concept of life (Jiva) and non-life (Ajiva) as a unique ontological framework that integrates consciousness, matter, space, and time.
To understand Jain classification of living beings — from one-sensed organisms to five-sensed beings — and its parallels with modern biological taxonomy and ecology.
To examine the scientific foresight in Jain thought, including the awareness of microorganisms, elemental life, and ecological interdependence long before modern discoveries.
To analyze the Jain doctrines of Karma, evolution, and Ahimsa as biological, ethical, and ecological principles shaping both inner and outer worlds of life.
To evaluate the relevance of Jain biological philosophy in addressing contemporary challenges such as sustainability, biodiversity conservation, and ethical science.
Unit III: Chemistry in Jainism ( 25 -36)
To understand the Jain conception of matter (Pudgala) as one of the six eternal substances, including its defining characteristics and role in the physical and metaphysical universe.
To study the atomic theory (Paramanu and Skandha) in Jain philosophy and explore its scientific parallels with modern physics, chemistry, and quantum concepts.
To analyze the transformations and states of matter — from subtle to gross forms — and their interactions through natural processes without invoking divine creation.
To examine the material nature of Karma and its functional mechanisms as a fine form of Pudgala influencing consciousness, behavior, and liberation.
To explore Jain contributions to early scientific thought, including cosmology, alchemy, thermodynamics, and medicinal chemistry, emphasizing ethical and ecological principles in scientific practice.
Unit IV: Physics in Jainism ( 37-48)
To introduce Jainism as a scientific and rational philosophy of existence, exploring its unique approach to reality, motion, matter, and time in comparison with modern physics.
To study the six non-living substances (Ajiva dravyas) — Dharma, Adharma, Ākāśa, Kāla, and Pudgala — and understand their roles in motion, rest, space, and temporal change within the Jain cosmological framework.
To analyze Jain doctrines such as Anekāntavāda (Multiplicity of Truth) and Svabhāva (self-nature) as foundational principles offering deep philosophical parallels with modern scientific theories like relativity, quantum mechanics, and conservation laws.
To explore the Jain conception of the cosmos (Lokākāśa) and its eternal, self-sustained nature, contrasting it with creator-based cosmologies and modern scientific cosmology.
To evaluate the continuing relevance of Jain physics in contemporary discussions on science, metaphysics, sustainability, and the harmony between spiritual insight and empirical inquiry.
Unit V: The Science of Knowledge and the Soul (49-60)
To introduce the foundational principles of Jain philosophy, emphasizing non-violence (Ahimsa), non-absolutism (Anekantavada), and self-discipline as pathways to spiritual and intellectual liberation.
To explore the Jain theory of knowledge (Jñāna) — its nature, types, and role in revealing the soul’s true essence and overcoming karmic obscuration.
To analyze the concept of the soul (Ātmā) as a conscious, eternal, and independent entity, and examine how karmic bondage affects its inherent purity and omniscience.
To study the epistemological framework of Jainism, including sources of knowledge (Pramāṇa), conditioned viewpoints (Syādvāda), and the doctrine of multiple perspectives (Anekantavada), in comparison with other Indian philosophical systems.
To evaluate the contemporary significance of Jain philosophy, applying its insights on knowledge, ethics, and self-realization to modern issues such as mental well-being, non-violence, and sustainable living.

title: JAIN MATHEMATICS — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course, which means this is a common prerequisite for any course in Jain mathematics studies.
Course Outcome: - Bridging Gaps: It could bridge the gap between ancient Jain philosophy and modern mathematical interpretations, which will increase a deeper understanding of mathematical principles across different time periods.
- Historical Context: It could provide valuable historical context for the development of mathematical thought, showing how some modern mathematical concepts may have roots in ancient Jain texts.
- New Insights: Examination of ancient Jain texts can inspire new research directions and innovative solutions to modern problems.
Curriculum: Unit I: Jain Mathematics: Introduction (1- 12)
- Learning the History of Mathematics. Knowledge of renowned mathematicians of Greek, Babylonian, Egypt and China.
- Contribution of Indian Mathematicians in the field of Mathematics.
- Awareness about Jainism and the roots of Mathematics in Jainism.
- Branches of studies in Jain literature.
- Jain School of Mathematics and specialities of Jain Mathematics.
Unit II: Jain Sources of Mathematics ( 13- 24)
- Students will be aware of the Jain Sources of Mathematics. They have knowledge regarding Karnanuyoga and their texts.
- Contribution of Jain Acharyas in the field of Mathematics.
- Mathematical concepts in the major Jain texts.
- Familiar with the current writers and scholars on Jain Mathematics. .
- Learn about Jain Logic.
Unit III: Specialities of Jain Mathematics (Basic) ( 25 -36)
- Student has awareness about ancient Indian wisdom in the field of Mathematics.
- Learner will learn the concepts of Place value system, Indices, Logarithms, Value of Pie, Permutation and Combinations and Mensuration according to Jain Mathematicians.
- Familiar with the language and concepts of ancient Indian texts.
Unit IV: Specialities of Jain Mathematics (Advance) ( 37-48)
This module provides learners with an in-depth examination of the extensive numerical systems in Jain Mathematics, including the symbolic notations utilized. Consequently, their rational and analytical capacities will be developed.
Unit V: Jain Astronomy and Cosmology (49-60)
- This course provides introduction and brief description of astronomy and cosmology in Jain philosophy and culture.
- Introduction may generate interest in learners for further research.
- Introduced learners with our ancient wisdom.
- Helpful for the further research.
- In ancient times mathematics is the offshoot of astronomy, its introduction may make concept more clear. An interdisciplinary way of learning make learners knowledge broad and exhaustive.

title: Indic Meta Thinking -2 — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): • To explore and analyze types of cognition, including valid and non-valid cognition, through the lens of Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS).
- To understand inference, syllogisms, and logical structures, enhancing critical thinking and reasoning abilities.
- To identify and address cognitive fallacies and discrepancies to improve intellectual clarity.
- To gain insights into the functioning of the mind (chitta) and its states, modifications, and distractions.
- To explore practical solutions like Shadanga Yoga and Kriya Yoga for attaining mental clarity and focus.
- To apply frameworks of Indic epistemology, including Shravana, Manana, and Nididhyasana, to achieve clarity in wisdom, speech, and action in real-life situations.
Course Outcome: • Analyze Cognitive Processes: Differentiate between valid and non-valid cognition and understand their respective processes, causes, and validations.

- Identify and Resolve Fallacies: Recognize and address cognitive fallacies (Hetvabhasa) to ensure clarity and accuracy in reasoning.
- Understand and Regulate the Mind: Examine the nature and states of chitta, understanding its modifications and distractions to achieve mental balance.
- Implement Yogic Practices for Clarity: Use Shadanga Yoga and Kriya Yoga techniques to improve focus and resolve cognitive discrepancies.
- Achieve Practical Wisdom: Integrate principles of Indic Meta Thinking to achieve clarity in thought, speech, and action, especially in challenging situations.

Building on the foundational concepts of Indic Meta Thinking - 1, this course delves deeper into the intricacies of cognition, inference, and logical structures, emphasizing their relevance in modern intellectual and practical contexts.
The course begins by examining the nature of cognition, distinguishing between valid (prama) and non-valid (bhrama) forms, and exploring their causes, processes, and validation techniques. It then transitions into understanding the systematic processes of inference (anumana) and syllogistic reasoning (pancha-avayava), equipping students with tools for structured and precise analysis. A significant focus is placed on identifying and addressing cognitive fallacies (hetvabhasa), ensuring clarity and sound reasoning.
Moving beyond theoretical insights, the course investigates the workings of the mind (chitta), its states, modifications, and distractions, to provide a deeper understanding of cognitive discrepancies. Solutions rooted in Indic traditions, such as Shadanga Yoga and Kriya Yoga, are explored to cultivate mental clarity and focus.
Finally, the course synthesizes these concepts to present the outcomes of Indic Meta Thinking, emphasizing practical frameworks like Shravana (listening), Manana (reflection), and Nididhyasana (meditation) for achieving clarity in thought, speech, and action. By integrating timeless wisdom with modern challenges, the course equips learners to navigate complexities with insight, balance, and precision.

title: Bharatiya Knowledge Ecosystem and Knowledge Models — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): The course aims to:
1. Introduce students to the foundational concepts, sources, and structures of Bharatiya knowledge systems.
2. Analyze the auxiliary sciences that supported ancient knowledge systems and their relevance in modern contexts.
3. Explore philosophical frameworks and their contribution to knowledge creation, interpretation, and application in governance.
4. Encourage critical thinking about the role of knowledge in societal well-being and governance.
5. Introduce model-based reasoning as a core scientific methodology and demonstrate its relevance to the study of ancient Indic knowledge systems.
6. Equip students with the skills to assess, build, and apply scientific models in both traditional and contemporary contexts.
7. Recontextualize Vedic śāstras as scientific models for use in modern real-world problems.
Course Outcome: Upon completion of the course, students will be able to:
1. Gain a comprehensive understanding of the Bharatiya knowledge ecosystem, including its philosophical, ritualistic, and textual foundations.
2. Understand the interconnectedness of knowledge, ethics, governance, and societal prosperity through both traditional and modern lenses.
3. Develop critical thinking on the relevance and application of ancient knowledge systems in contemporary governance and societal structures.
4. Build and assess robust scientific models for simulating real-world systems using both modern and traditional approaches.
5. Recontextualize Vedic śāstras as models with scientific applications, contributing to contemporary discourse on knowledge and its applications.
6. Apply model-based reasoning to interpret traditional texts and integrate these with modern scientific methods for academic and real-world solutions.
Curriculum: Unit 1: Foundations of Bharatiya Knowledge Ecosystem Concepts of Knowledge:
Explore traditional Bharatiya concepts of knowledge (Jñāna and Vijñāna) and their transformation in modern contexts. Examine the evolution of key terms like ‘knowledge’, ‘skills’, and ‘education’.
Sources of Knowledge:
Study oral traditions, manuscripts, and written texts as sources of knowledge. Analyze how these contribute to ancient and contemporary systems of knowledge.
Vedic Texts and Interpretations:
Discuss the structure, classification, and interpretation of Vedic texts. Compare ancient and modern interpretations and their role in current thought.
Knowledge in Rituals:
Examine how rituals and ancient texts mutually influence one another and shape Bharatiya knowledge systems.
Classification of Knowledge:
Traditional classifications of knowledge in the Indian context, such as the 64 fields of knowledge and the distinction between Sāttvika, Rājasika, and Tāmasika knowledge.
Unit 2: Auxiliary Sciences and Their Contemporary Relevance
Phonetics, Linguistics, and Metrics:
Study ancient systems of phonetics and linguistics and their modern relevance. Explore the role of prosody in the preservation of oral texts and its contribution to mathematics.
Semantics and Hermeneutics:
Analyze the interpretation of meaning in ancient texts, focusing on how these systems influence modern semantics and cognitive studies.
Mathematics and Geometry in Rituals:
Explore the mathematical underpinnings of rituals and their connections to geometry, binary systems, and the concept of zero.
Astronomy and Meteorology:
Examine the ancient Indian understanding, particularly in relation to modern fields such as astronomy, linguistics etc.
Unit 3: Interpretative Frameworks and Philosophical Systems
Philosophical Systems:
Study key philosophical schools like Mimamsa, Vedanta, Nyaya, Vaiseshika, Sankhya, and Yoga, focusing on their applications in contemporary philosophy, psychology, and ethics.
Interpretation of Ancient Texts:
Investigate traditional methods of textual interpretation and their relevance in modern knowledge management, linguistic analysis, and cognitive science.
Epic and Narrative Literature:
Examine how epics like the Mahabharata and Ramayana act as repositories of knowledge and offer insights into governance, ethics, and social structures.
Indic Models of Knowledge in Aesthetics, Health, and Public Administration:
Analyze the traditional models of knowledge in various domains such as Arthashastra (governance), Natya Shastra (aesthetics), and Ayurveda (health).
Unit 4: The Process of Knowledge Creation
What is Knowledge and Knowledge Systems?
Distinguish between knowledge (as information) and knowledge systems (as processes of extracting knowledge).
Introduction to Science:
Define science and its distinction from art. Discuss the empirical and theoretical bases of scientific inquiry.
Methods and Tools of Science:
Explore model building, strengths, and limitations of scientific inquiry, as well as the subjective element in science.
Approximate vs. Exact Sciences:
Study the distinction between approximate and exact sciences and the implications of this difference for model-based reasoning.
Strengths and Limits of Scientific Inquiry:
Discuss the scope of scientific investigation and its applicability to real-world problems.
Unit 5: Model-Based Reasoning in Scientific Thinking
Models as Representations of Reality:
Understand models as compact representations of observed reality. Study different types of models: Top-Down, Bottom-Up, and Hybrid models.
Purpose and Methods of Modelling:
Investigate abstraction and classification as methods of modelling. Learn how models are used to explain, predict, and control reality.
Anatomy of a Model:
Analyze the components of a model, including the states of entities, structural and functional relations among concepts, and the actions that trigger state transitions.
Assessing the Quality of a Model:
Learn criteria for evaluating models and their effectiveness in answering questions related to knowledge systems.
Traditional and Modern Knowledge Models:
Discuss how traditional Bharatiya knowledge models can be integrated with modern scientific frameworks for a holistic understanding of knowledge.

title: Indic Vision for Human Society — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): Encourage understanding of "Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam"
Explore human existence's connection to the cosmos. Foster responsibility and participation for an inclusive society.
Provide insights into ancient Indian knowledge for holistic well-being
Offer holistic insights from ancient Indian knowledge for overall well-being of individuals and societies.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course, students will be able to:
Understand the Bharatiya perspectives on human society.
Explore the fundamental principles of Indian philosophy.
Appreciate the aims of human life according to Indian traditions.
Analyze the practical applications of Indian wisdom in various fields.
Develop a deep understanding of the Indian vision for societal harmony and individual purpose.
Curriculum: Unit I: Bharatiya Perspectives - The World View & Vision of Human Society and Aspiration (Modules 1 to 17)
Introduction to non-duality in Prakriti (Jad) and Purush (Chetana).
The five great elements (Pancha-mahabhutas) and their significance.
Understanding the root of sorrow and suffering.
The pursuit of salvation and eternal peace.
Acceptance and complementariness of various philosophical systems in ancient India.
The Four Purusarthas: Dharma, Artha, Kama, Moksha.
Concepts of Abhyudaya and Nihsreyasa.
Ancient texts and laws: Dharma Sutras and Shastra.
Stages of life: Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha, Sannyasa.

Understanding Atman-Brahman.
Shiksha Valli and Bhrigu Valli studies.
The concept of Koshas and four states of consciousness.
The importance of awareness and Prana.
Unit III: Balancing Knowledge and Life - Individual and Social Harmony (23 to 30)
Vidya vs. Avidya.
The balance of Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas.
Patanjali's Yoga Sutras.
Saadhana Chatushtayam and types of Karma.
Meditation and paths of yoga for societal harmony.

title: Science of Art and Aesthetics — Objectives & Outcomes
Science of Art and Aesthetics — Curriculum
content:
About the Course | This course offers a comprehensive exploration of Indian Aesthetics, juxtaposed with Western perspectives, to provide a holistic understanding of aesthetic principles.
It delves into the Vedic and Upanishadic foundations of beauty, the philosophical underpinnings of aesthetics, and the comparative analysis of subjective and objective elements in aesthetic appreciation.
The curriculum includes a deep dive into the Nāṭyaśāstra’s dramatic theories, the balance between realism and idealism in art, and the application of design thinking in aesthetic creation. Through a blend of theoretical study and practical analysis, learners will engage with the aesthetics of nature, art, and literature, culminating in a nuanced understanding of the essence of aesthetic experience.
Learning Objectives | To understand the foundational principles of Eastern and Western aesthetics.
To analyze the Vedic and Upanishadic conceptions of beauty and bliss.
To explore the evolution of Western aesthetics from classical to contemporary times.
To critically examine the philosophical foundations that underpin aesthetic theories.
To compare and contrast the notions of subjectivity and objectivity across cultures.
Intended Outcome | Learners will be able to:
Articulate the key differences and similarities between Eastern and Western aesthetic principles.
Gain the ability to apply Vedic and Upanishadic ideas to contemporary discussions of nature and art.
Develop a critical lens for analyzing various aesthetic philosophies and their relevance to modern contexts.
Integrate design thinking with aesthetic theory to innovate in the fields of creativity and design.
