title: The Science and Art of Music — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): 1. This is a Discipline specific course on understanding music as an art and a knowledge system.
2. The course focuses on detailing the musical principles and ideas delineated in the Sangita Ratnakara, a musical treatise authored in the 13th CE, treating it as a reference point to discuss and understand the development of Indian music through the centuries.
3. The course examines contemporary Karnataka music practice in light of changes in nomenclature, musical ideas, melodic forms, etc., relating them to the Ratnakara and other significant music texts of later periods.
Course Outcome: • To know about Karnataka music from a historical perspective and understand the development of music through different periods.
- To know how to approach the knowledge system of music and understand the essentiality of practice as a precedent to musical thinking and analysis.
- To see how contemporary practice bears threads of continuity to the musical knowledge and ideas discussed in 1300 CE while recognizing the changes that help the practice retain its dynamism.
- The listening activities in the course modules help in cognition of the sound and aesthetic of Karnataka music.
Curriculum: Unit 1 Introduction to Indian music and musicology (1 to 10)
- A brief outline of the development of Indian music from the chants of the Samaveda, in six stages
- Understanding the terms ‘science’ and ‘art’ in the context of Indian music research.
- Development of musicology and music Research in the Indian music tradition.
- A note on some important music texts, Sangita Ratnakara in particular.
- Connotation of the words ‘sangita’ and ‘gita’.
- Importance of gita, the vocal music aspect, and its universal appeal.
- ‘nada’ or the musical sound that manifests in the human body; three main perspectives of nada manifestation namely physiological, yogic, and philosophical.
- Description of the melodic units of sruti and svara.
- Different kinds of description of ‘svara’, like association with animal and bird sounds, etc.
- Classification of svara as vadi, samvadi, etc.
- Rasa-s associated with svara-s.
- Categorising svara-s in an octave as suddha and vikrta.
- Organisation of tonal structures like grama, murchana and tana.
Unit 2 Understanding tonal forms, basics of raga, and the raga systems in Carnatic music (11 to 20)
- Description of varna as a tonal form in the Ratnakara and the compositional form varna as seen in current practice of Karnataka music
- The term alankara as described in Ratnakara, then in Caturdandi Prakasika and as seen in contemporary practice
- Exposition of raga in the Ratnakara
- Marga and desi raga-s and the two types of classifications of raga-s into grama raga, etc. and raganga, bhashanga, etc.
- Method of description of raga-s with illustrations in the Ratnakara
- Development of the mela-janya system of raga classification
- The 72 melakarta scheme and its features
- A note on the raganga raga and melakarta raga systems, their similarities and differences
- Janya raga-s and their types
Unit 3 Types of raga classifications; other important aspects of music in the Ratnakara period and contemporary Carnatic music practice ( 21 to 30)
- Some other kinds of raga classifications
- Description of music practitioners – composers, singers and their types.
- Types of voices, the singing voice and types of musical performances.
- Description of some musical aspects like gamaka, alapti, etc and their connotations in contemporary practice.
- A brief outline of tala-s described in the Sangita Ratnakara.
- Description of the 108 tala-s, suladi sapta tala-s and other kinds of tala-s like capu, that are employed in current practice.
- A brief note on the four types of instruments and how instruments in contemporary times relate to each of the four types described in the Ratnakara.
- A brief note on the chapter on dance in the Ratnakara.
- Details of the compositional forms described in the Ratnakara – particularly, prabandha.
- Description of compositional or kalpita and creative or manodharma forms found in current Carnatic music practice.

title: The Science and Art of Music — Curriculum
content: General Information about the curriculum: This course gives an introduction to various aspects of Karnataka music in particular and Indian music in general. It helps the learner to understand music from historic, musical and technical perspectives both in terms of the contemporary practice of Karnataka music and shastra-based thought processes. The course includes listening activities that will help the learner to experience the melody and aesthetics of Karnataka music, and thereby emphasises the need to be able to recognise tonal patterns and melodic forms of the rendition in order to understand the technical and shastraic aspects of the knowledge system.

title: Basic Principles of Arthashastra — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): 1. Understanding Artha: To explore the concept of 'artha' beyond material wealth, encompassing objectives, purposes, and societal welfare, and its significance in Bharateeya culture.
2. Legacy and Evolution: To discuss the historical development of the Artha Shastra texts, including contributions from Chanakya and previous scholars like Sukracharya and Brhaspati.
3. Timeless Principles: To examine the enduring relevance of Artha Shastra's principles in contemporary governance, ethical administration, and balanced societal prosperity.
4. Comparative Analysis: To analyze how Artha Shastra's pragmatic approach contrasts with modern democratic and human rights-focused governance models.
5. Practical Applications: To apply key concepts like 'Nyaya' (means of administration) and 'Dharma' (administration) in modern-day scenarios for effective societal and individual administration.
Course Outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Comprehend Key Concepts: Understand the broad concept of 'artha' and its implications in societal welfare and governance.
2. Appreciate Historical Context: Recognize the historical evolution and legacy of Artha Shastra, and the contributions of key ancient scholars.
3. Apply Ancient Wisdom: Utilize the timeless principles of Artha Shastra in modern governance and administrative contexts.
4. Analyze Governance Models: Critically compare the Artha Shastra's approach to statecraft and economic policy with contemporary governance models.
5. Implement Ethical Practices: Implement ethical and balanced approaches in leadership and decision-making processes inspired by the teachings of Artha Shastra.

title: Principles of Intuitive Awareness – Basics — Curriculum
content:
General Information about the curriculum: Intuition can be defined as the ability to tune into knowledge that is beyond the scope of our five senses and the mind. Intuitive awareness is crucial for maximizing human potential and personal productivity and well-being, as well as all-round societal welfare. The relevance of this is being gradually rediscovered in the modern era. However, this knowledge was deeply rooted in the Indian śāstras and is the very foundation of Indian Knowledge Systems. This course will combine modern and traditional Indian perspectives to introduce the basic principles of intuitive awareness and its relevance at the personal level.

title: Indian Knowledge Systems and Traditions — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): The course provides a background to Indian knowledge systems and traditions and their relevance in the fields of sciences, technology, literature and arts. Key highlights include:
- Curated for all academic disciplines as a foundational program
- Enables understanding of India’s knowledge framework, its genesis, evolution and key components
- The course is an essential first-step before deep-dive into discipline-specific concepts aligned with various career fields
Course Outcome: ● Know the structure, hierarchy and classifications of Indian knowledge systems
- Overview of specific areas of Indian traditional knowledge, architecture and arts
- Appreciate the contributions made by Indian Knowledge systems in some of the technical fields such as mineralogy, mechanics etc.

Program educational Objective(s): 1. Engaging in thoughtful expression using Samskrit language.
2. Understanding the structure of simple samskrit sentences. Introduction to the devanagari script. Enjoying the ancient simple and famous texts through original language.

title: Philosophy of Language — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be a foundation course, which means this is a common prerequisite for any course in Indic knowledge studies.
Course Outcome: As a result of this course, the student will gain an appreciation of what the Vedas say about the speech of all creatures, the fundamental process of articulation that produces the different types of phonemes, the nature of word and meaning and their relation, the four different levels of Vaak or language, the theory of sphota as enunciated by Bhartrhari, the difference between normal and poetic language and an introduction to the great Vyakarana tradition of India.
Curriculum: Lesson 1 - Introduction to Language in Sanskrit Tradition
- Types of Vak in the Vedas – sounds in nature, that of animals and human language
- Four out of Six Vedangas deal with language
- Vyakarana in India was most advanced science of linguistics in the world
- Early grammarian traditions prior to and after Panini
Lesson 2 - Theory of śabda – sound & word
- Nature of sound – what is nitya
- Sound is produced by samyoga, vibhaga and sabda
- Articulate and Inarticulate sounds
- Phonetics and types of phonemes
- What is a word?
- Nature of meaning
- Relation between word and meaning
- Concept of Pravahanityata in Vyakarana
LESSON 3 - The Power of the Word
- What is the denotative power of a word
- Relation between word and meaning is pratyayya-pratyayaka sambandha
- Does the word refer to a category or universal?
- Does a word refer to an individual?
- Relation between class category (universal) and individual
- Apoha theory of the Buddhists
LESSON 4 – Usage of word and sentence – Vrtti & Vakya
- What is the primary meaning of words
- Abhidha or sakti
- Secondary meaning of words – lakshana
- Conditions for secondary meaning of words
- Suggested meaning or Vyanjana
- Use of Vyanjana in poetry

- Abhihitanvayavada, Anvitabhidhana
LESSON 6 – The Fourfold Division of Vak

title: Indian Psychology: An Integral Model of Human Experience — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): The program shall enable learners to:
1. Develop a comprehensive understanding of human psychology by integrating Western theories with Vedic perspectives from sources like Ayurveda, Jyotisha, and Yoga.
2. Gain knowledge of human growth and development through psychological theories and Vedic principles, focusing on life stages and their psychological traits.
3. Acquire practical skills in Vedic psychological diagnosis and apply interventions such as Pranic healing, Yogasana, and Hypnotherapy in therapy.
4. Explore and critically evaluate Western and Vedic personality theories to understand factors shaping identity, behavior, and social interaction.
Build foundational counselling skills using both Vedic and Western approaches to support psychological well-being.
5. Examine social behavior and cultural influences on psychology, integrating both perspectives for a holistic view of human interaction.
Course Outcome: After completion of this course students will be able to -
1. Comprehend the basic meaning & nature of western psychology
2. Compare and contrast various paradigms of western psychology
3. Understand and evaluate various fundamental concepts of Vedic psychology
4. Juxtapose western and Vedic understanding of human personality
5. Diagnose various psychological issues and create an intervention plan by integrating western and Vedic principles
Target Audience: This is intended to be offered as a foundation course across all UG programs both STEM and non-STEM.

title: Indic Predictive Science Advanced — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is a semi-advanced course for astrology students, designed to provide an overview and broaden their understanding of the subject, preparing them for more advanced studies.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course, the student will gain:
Exposure and Awareness: Learners will gain profound exposure to and awareness of various branches within Indic predictive sciences, such as Medical Astrology, Agricultural Astrology, Water Divination, Weather Forecasting, Disaster Predictions, Vastu Shastra, Samskaras, Muhurta Shastra, Human Relationships, and Remedies.
Contemporary Relevance: Learners will understand how these branches of Jyotisha are relevant and applicable in modern contexts, addressing present-day challenges in healthcare, agriculture, environmental management, and personal well-being.
Intellectual Enrichment: The course will broaden learners' intellectual horizons by introducing them to ancient wisdom embedded in predictive sciences, deepening their appreciation and understanding of the Indian knowledge system.
Holistic Perspective: Learners will be inspired to adopt a holistic view of Indic predictive sciences, recognizing how interconnected disciplines like astrology, vastu, and other traditional practices offer comprehensive insights into health, relationships, and the natural world.
Curriculum: Unit I: Prear Knowledge
- History of Astrology.
Panchanga Knowlende
Basic calculations in Muhurata(Electional Astrology)
Unit II: Usage of Predictive Science in mundane life
- over view of different types of Samskaras and
- Methods of calculating Marriage Compatibility.
Unit III: Human Personality from Jyotisha
- Human-Relationship: Influence of planetary positions on relationships and compatibility.
- Stri-Jataka: Astrological factors affecting women's personalities and life paths.
-Yogas: Effects of planetary combinations on character traits and challenges.
- Planetary Conjunction: Impact of planets in the same zodiac sign on behavior and life events.
- Education: Indicators of intellectual ability and educational success.
- Career Planning: Astrological guidance for career potential and milestones.
Unit 4: Variety of Applications
- Spiritual Astrology: Exploration of astrological insights into spiritual growth, enlightenment, and the connection between planetary influences and personal spiritual journeys.
- Medical Astrology: Study of planetary positions in diagnosing health issues and understanding their impact on physical and mental well-being.
- Agricultural Astrology: Application of astrology to farming practices, including ideal planting times, crop success, and livestock health based on planetary influences.
- Vastu: Examination of traditional architectural principles and how they align with planetary influences to create harmonious living spaces.
- Water Deriving: Techniques for identifying water sources using astrological insights and planetary influences related to water elements.
- Defence Strategy: The role of astrology in formulating strategies for national defense, security, and conflict resolution.
- Disaster Predictions: Astrological methods for predicting natural disasters like earthquakes, floods, and fires, along with their timing and intensity
- Weather Forecasting: Use of astrology to predict weather patterns and climatic changes, aiding in agricultural planning and disaster preparedness.
Unit V: Other topics
Ayanamsa: Concept of Ayanamsa and its calculations
Modern Science: Astrological insights in Modern science
Remedies: Astrological Remedies in mundane human problems

title: Indic Meta Thinking -1 — Curriculum
content:
General Information about the curriculum: Meta thinking, often referred to as metacognition, is the act of thinking about thinking. It involves being aware of and understanding one's own thought processes, strategies, and cognitive abilities. Meta thinking allows individuals to monitor, analyze, and regulate their thinking in order to improve learning, problem-solving, decision-making, and overall cognitive performance. It involves reflecting on one's own cognitive strengths and weaknesses, recognizing biases and assumptions, and adapting strategies to achieve better outcomes. In essence, meta-thinking is about being mindful of how you think and utilizing that awareness to enhance cognitive abilities and optimize mental processes.
This course comprehensively explores methodologies, processes and many more related to meta thinking encapsulated in various disciplines of Indian Knowledge Sysytems. This course sheds light on thought and its profound impact on shaping human society. Through examining the core principles that have guided one of the world's oldest civilizations, students will gain insights into the timeless concepts and their relevance in the modern world.

title: Textile Traditions of Rural and Tribal India — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is meant to be an elective course, which can taken by the UG students of different subjects
Course Outcome: •            To detailing different traditional textiles from vary corners of the country so that students can get knowledge regarding the rich history and heritage of textile traditions of India.
-             To provide knowledge about different design patterns and styles of weaving, by which students can be benefited with rich knowledge of Indian textile industry.
-             To enable the students about cultural diversities of Indian textile industry which groom the current generation towards ‘beauty lies with diversity’ rather than mass consumerism for ‘one-size-fit-for all’.
-             To enrich the Indian students towards cultural sustainability through symbolic values of different design patterns and thus creating Indianness by which cultural sustainability can be achieved.

-             Comparative Analysis among major textiles in India

Implemented development programmes for development of textile industry and its effectiveness

-             Sustainability challenges to textiles: Environment, Health and Culture
-             Traditional Textile Knowledge System in India
The emerging economic models and their alignment with traditional practices

-             Cultural identity of different product design

content:
Program educational Objective(s): To provide students with a comprehensive understanding of the agricultural practices described in the ancient Krishi shastras, emphasizing the practical application using Jyotisha in agriculture. Students will learn the historical context, importance, and practical techniques for farming, seed preparation, sowing, irrigation, and harvesting as guided by ancient Indian wisdom.
Course Outcome: By the end of this course, students will be able to:
1. Understand the historical and cultural significance of "Krishi Shastra" and the integration of Jyotisha in agriculture.

5. Apply knowledge of nakshatras to optimize planting times and methods.
6. Implement traditional rituals associated with farming.
7. Manage irrigation, water preservation, and field preparation techniques.
8. Execute traditional harvesting and seed preservation methods.

Unit 1: (Modules 1–8): Roots of Indian Agriculture and the Vedic Cosmos
This unit explores the origins of agriculture in Indian civilization, its integration with Vedic knowledge, and how early societies intertwined farming with cosmology and spiritual practices. It begins with an overview of agriculture's role in ancient India, including the societal importance of farmers and the historical occurrences of famine. Learners are introduced to the philosophical foundations of astrology, particularly its origins in the Vedas, and its essential role in supporting agrarian life. The unit emphasizes how astrology was not merely predictive but a deeply respected tool for timing and decision-making, governing everything from sowing to harvesting. Insights from sacred texts like the Śrī Rudram offer a spiritual and cultural lens into how crops were perceived as divine gifts.
Unit 2 (Modules 9–20): Astrological Influences on Weather, Water, and Land
This unit dives into the astrological and environmental systems that influence agricultural decision-making. Students develop an understanding of the Navagrahas (nine planetary influences) and how their positions correlate with climate changes, crop cycles, and land productivity. Concepts like Nakshatras, Rashis, and Nava Nayakas are introduced to explain the cosmic blueprint of seasons and soil types. Ancient methods of weather prediction, rainfall calculation, and water conservation are explored through both astrological knowledge and field observation techniques. The unit also covers monsoon forecasting, water divining practices, and the role of the zodiac in determining land characteristics and suitability for specific crops. Learners develop a toolkit of traditional and cosmic methods to predict and respond to environmental shifts affecting agriculture.
Unit 3 (Modules 21–28): Timing, Rituals, and Sustainable Practices in Vedic Agriculture
In this unit, learners apply their foundational and cosmic understanding to practical agricultural methods. Emphasis is placed on timing agricultural activities—like ploughing, sowing, and harvesting—using astrological guidance, particularly auspicious Yogas, Tithis, and planetary alignments. Students explore how traditional tools and rituals were structured to enhance yield and maintain harmony with nature. This includes the sequence of farming tasks, post-harvest management, and how timing decisions were derived from Panchanga (Vedic calendar). The unit culminates in a reflection on the Indian Knowledge System’s holistic role in agriculture, integrating astrology, Vastu, Ayurveda, and ecological wisdom to form a sustainable, spiritually aligned farming model that has endured for millennia.

title: Ayurveda: The Science of Wellness- Basic — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): This is a basic-level course that will introduce you to the fundamental principles and key concepts of Ayurveda.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course the student will gain;
1. Exposure and Awareness: Learners will gain a profound exposure to and awareness of the principles of Ayurveda according to Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita.
2. Contemporary Relevance: Learners will understand how Ayurvedic teachings are relevant and applicable in modern times, bridging the gap between ancient wisdom and current challenges.
3. Intellectual Enrichment: The course will enrich learners’ intellectual horizons, expanding their understanding and appreciation of Ayurveda.
4. Holistic Perspective: Learners will be inspired to develop a holistic approach to life and its components as well as acquire an Indic perspective on health and wellbeing.
Curriculum: Unit I-a: Introduction to Ayurveda (6)
- History and Philosophy of Ayurveda: Overview of the origin and evolution of Ayurveda, available literature, its objective, the foundational concept of 'Trisutra' (Ayurveda in a nutshell) and its purpose in and relevance to modern society. • Decoding 'Trisutra' in detail. Definition of 'Swastha', health, and its characteristics.
- Examination of terminologies such as 'Ayu' and 'Ayurveda,' and the principle called 'Tridanda Siddhanta'.
- Gross understanding of the eight limbs of Ayurveda, i.e., 'Ashtanga Ayurveda' and expanding the 6 'Padarthas': 'Samanya Vishesha Siddhanta', the theory of similarity and speciality, with various examples to learn its application. Brief note on 'Loka Purusha Samya Vada'.
- Strengthening basic vocabulary: 'Guna', 'Karma' and Dravya'. Learning about the nine primordial substances 'Nava Karana Dravyas' (including 'Panchamahabhuta Siddhanta'), twenty qualities 'Vimshati gunas'. • Summarizing the purpose of Ayurveda through well established principles learned thus far. 'Dhatu Samya'
Unit I-b: Key Concepts of Ayurveda (6)
- Using the basic vocabulary and principles to build on core concepts. 'Tridosha Siddhanta': gross location of doshas, and their 'guna' and 'karma'. Brief note on Manasika doshas.
- 'The Doshik Clock': establishing the relationship between predominance of doshas and time, age, and digestion.
- Understanding 'Agni' and 'Koshta' with respect to body constitution 'Prakriti'. Formation and types of 'Prakriti'. • Concept of 'Dhatu' and 'Mala': with application of 'Samanya Vishesha Siddhanta'. Relationship between 'Dosha' and 'Dhatu' • Understanding 'Rasa', its origin, types, qualities and actions, and its relation with 'Doshas', 'Dhatus', 'Panchamahabhutas', and digestion. Basic knowledge of 'Virya' and 'Vipaka'. • Classification of 'Dravyas', understanding 'Desha' with respect to 'Dosha'.
Unit II-a: Disease and Management Principles (6)
- Classification of 'Rogas' based on prognosis.
- 'Padachatushtayam' the 4 pillars to management of disease.
- 'Trividha hetu' understanding the root cause of illness.
- Examination of 'Roga', disease, and 'Rogi', diseased with examples.
- ‘Achara Rasayana’ A holistic mantra for maintenance of health.
- Ultimate treatments for each 'Dosha'. Agrya Dravyas
Unit II-b: Dosha-wise treatment (5)
- 'Dvividhopakramaniya' Two types of Treatment and connecting to 'Samanya Vishesha Siddhanta'.
- 'Vata' treatment
- 'Pitta' treatment
- 'Kapha' treatment
Unit III-a: Holistic Wellness (3)
- Components of a Holistic treatment. (daiva, yukti, sattvavajaya)
- Principles of managing Mental Illness • Expanding 'Trividha Ayatana' Importance of appropriate union. 'Samyak Yoga'
Unit III-b: How to Manage Personal life with Ayurveda (5)
- 'Tisraishaniya' Three desires of life. • 'Trayopasthambha': 'Ahara' • 'Nidra' and 'Abrahmacharya' • How to achieve the 3 desires with the support of three pillars? 'Dinacharya' and 'Rutucharya'.

- Using the basic vocabulary and principles to build on core concepts. 'Tridosha Siddhanta': gross location of doshas, and their 'guna' and 'karma'. Brief note on Manasika doshas.

- 'Padachatushtayam' the 4 pillars to management of disease.
- 'Trividha hetu' understanding the root cause of illness.

- Ultimate treatments for each 'Dosha'. Agrya Dravyas

- 'Dvividhopakramaniya' Two types of Treatment and connecting to 'Samanya Vishesha Siddhanta'.
- 'Vata' treatment
- 'Pitta' treatment
- 'Kapha' treatment
Unit III-a: Holistic Wellness (3)
- Components of a Holistic treatment. (daiva, yukti, sattvavajaya)
- Principles of managing Mental Illness • Expanding 'Trividha Ayatana' Importance of appropriate union. 'Samyak Yoga'
Unit III-b: How to Manage Personal life with Ayurveda (5)
- 'Tisraishaniya' Three desires of life. • 'Trayopasthambha': 'Ahara' • 'Nidra' and 'Abrahmacharya' • How to achieve the 3 desires with the support of three pillars? 'Dinacharya' and 'Rutucharya'.

title: Samskrit 3 - Technical Literature — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): 1) Analyze and understand complex sentences.
2) Explain how various technical texts are structured.
3) Identify important elements of different types of texts.
Course Outcome: Upon successful completion of this course, students will be able to: 1) Understand the meaning of sentences by identifying action-denoting words and associating various words with them.

Course Highlights: Model based reasoning is the hallmark of all sciences. A model is a compact representation of a real-world system that makes it amenable to explain, predict and control the system. A model consists of concepts and their relationships. Abstraction and classification are the techniques used to extract concepts from the system.
However, deriving the concepts is non-trivial. A system can be viewed in multiple ways resulting in a variety of models. To arrive at a sound model which represents the system accurately, we need a methodology that views the system.
Shaastras provide such models of real-world phenomena, but the concepts they embed are derived using standard perspectives common across all shaastras. These perspectives are provided by Vedic darshanas. Understanding the darshanas enables one to understand the abstractions of shaastric models accurately. We call these perspectives as thought models. There are 4 thought models Nyaaya-Vaiseshika, Sankhya-Yoga, Vyaakarana, and Miimaansa. In the current course, we explore the Bharatiya darshana-s, namely, Nyaaya and Saankhya, to assimilate their dRShti-s or worldviews and their thought models.
To introduce 2 main vedic darshanas Nyaaya-Vaisheshika and Saankhya-Yoga, and extract the modeling paradigm they use in analyzing the world.
To show how it can be applied in modeling any other topic.
To give 2 different perspectives for creating scientific models.

title: Ayurveda: The Science of Wellness- Advanced — Objectives & Outcomes
content:
Program educational Objective(s): The prerequisite for this course is 'Ayurveda: The Science of Wellness- Basic' [SKF-DC-1026-1]. This course is an advanced-level course, an extension of the basic course that builds on the principles and concepts learned thus far.
Course Outcome: At the end of the course the student will gain;
1. Exposure and Awareness: Learners will gain a profound exposure to and awareness of the Ayurvedic practices according to Charaka Samhita and Sushruta Samhita.
2. Contemporary Relevance: Learners will understand how Ayurvedic rituals are relevant and applicable in modern times, bridging the gap between ancient wisdom and current challenges.
3. Intellectual Enrichment: The course will enrich learners’ intellectual horizons, expanding their understanding and appreciation of Ayurveda.
4. Self Development: Learners will be inspired to develop a holistic approach to improve personal and professional life.

- Establishing an Ayurvedic daily routine by connecting to 'The Doshic Clock'
- 'Brahma Muhurta': A Wake-up Call. Rituals to do after waking up to manifest a life of abundance and peace.

- 'Vastradharana': An Ayurvedic Makeover. Clothing and accessories for healthy living.

- 'Ritucharya': Seasonal Resilience. Understanding the seasonal changes and appreciating the influence of 'Doshas' on the external environment and the human body.

- 'Vasanta': The Fruits of Spring. Recommended delicacies, activities, and therapies for the Spring season.
- 'Grishma': Surviving the Summers. Recommended delicacies, activities, and therapies for the Summer season.
- 'Varsha': Drenched in Monsoons. Recommended delicacies, activities, and therapies for the Rainy season.
- 'Sharat': Calm Down with Fall. Recommended delicacies, activities, and therapies for the Autumn season.

- 'Ahara Vidhi Visheshayatanas': Factors influencing the Effects of Food. The factors responsible for wholesome and unwholesome effects of food including method of food consumption.

- 'Pathya Ahara': Wholesome Food
- 'Viruddha Ahara': Incompatible Food

Course Description: This course offers a lateral understanding of Indian Knowledge Systems focusing on science and technology. Through a series of modules covering diverse topics such as physics, chemistry, mathematics, metallurgy, astronomy, architecture, textiles, agriculture, and transportation, students will explore the richness of ancient Indian scientific thought and technological advancements. Drawing upon historical texts, archaeological findings, and scholarly research, students will understand the principles, methodologies, and practical applications of ancient Indian science, gaining insights into its profound impact on global knowledge systems. By examining the legacy of Indian scholars and their contributions to human civilization, this course aims to promote a deep appreciation for the richness and diversity of Indian intellectual heritage.
Course Description: Indian Culture and Civilization is a comprehensive course that studies the heritage of Indian Knowledge Systems, exploring ancient Indian contributions across various domains such as philosophy, science, technology, mathematics, astronomy, linguistics, architecture, and social sciences. The course provides an overview of traditional Indian texts, systems, and practices, highlighting their historical development, cultural significance, and contemporary relevance.
Intended Objectives: To study the principles of Indian Knowledge Systems.
To understand the significant advancements made by ancient Indian mathematicians and astronomers, including their methodologies and innovations.
To examine ancient Indian approaches to health, wellness, architecture, and town planning, and understand their relevance and application in contemporary contexts.

1. The ability to decipher complex Samaasas is a crucial skill developed through Module II, enabling students to analyze compound words in Sanskrit sentences.
2. An attitude of meticulous examination is fostered in Module V, where students delve into the study of Balaramayanam, carefully scrutinizing 43 selected shlokas for a comprehensive understanding.
3. Throughout the course, students cultivate an attitude of linguistic precision, particularly evident in Module IV, where they learn the methodology to understand sentences, emphasizing accurate interpretation.
4. The ability to identify and apply krt and taddhita suffixes is honed in Module III, empowering students with linguistic tools essential for the analysis of Sanskrit texts.
5. An attitude of continuous learning and improvement is fostered through the formative assessment approach, ensuring that students actively engage with assignments and quizzes to enhance their understanding.
6. Module I focus on developing the ability to apply Vibhaktis effectively, allowing students to grasp the nuances of grammatical relationships within sentences.
7. An attitude of linguistic curiosity is encouraged throughout the curriculum, inspiring students to explore the intricacies of Sanskrit grammar and literature.
8. The ability to transform sentences, as taught in Module IV, equips students with a valuable skill set for interpreting and expressing ideas in Sanskrit with precision.
9. An attitude of critical analysis is instilled in the study of Balaramayanam in Module V, where students are encouraged to examine shlokas with a discerning eye, considering nuances of meaning.
10. The course aims to install an attitude of independent research, empowering students with the ability to delve into dictionaries and texts for a deeper understanding of krt and taddhita suffixes in Shastras.
Course Outcome: After attending this course, the student will be able to:
1. Demonstrate Proficiency in Analysing Sanskrit Sentences:
- At the conclusion of the course, students will be able to explain and analyze simple Sanskrit sentences, showcasing a comprehensive understanding of grammatical structures, including the usage of Vibhaktis, Sandhi, and Samaasa.
2. Apply Knowledge of Samaasa and Compound Word Formation:
- Students will develop the ability to identify and categorize different types of Samaasas, demonstrating proficiency in understanding compound word structures. This outcome emphasizes a practical application of linguistic knowledge in analyzing complex Sanskrit expressions.
3. Utilize Krt and Taddhita Suffixes in Shastras:
- By the end of the course, students will acquire the ability to recognize and utilize commonly used krt and taddhita suffixes in Shastric texts. This learning outcome focuses on practical skills in decoding and interpreting specific linguistic elements within Sanskrit literature.
4. Employ Methodology for Sentence Understanding:
- Students will develop an attitude of methodical examination and the ability to apply systematic methodologies for understanding Sanskrit sentences. This outcome emphasizes the cultivation of analytical skills and linguistic precision in the interpretation of both prose and poetic literature.
5. **Engage in Critical Analysis of Selected Texts:**
- Through the study of Balaramayanam and the analysis of 43 selected shlokas, students will develop **an attitude of** critical analysis. This learning outcome encourages students to critically examine the chosen texts, discerning subtle nuances in padavi-bhāga, sandhi, samāsa, and pratyayas, thereby fostering a deeper appreciation for Sanskrit literature.
Curriculum: Unit I - Usage of Vibhaktis:
- Understanding the application of Vibhaktis in sentences.
- Analysis of Karaka and Upapada Vibhaktis.
- Exploration of Sati-Saptami and Visheshya-Visheshana relationships.
- Application of Vibhaktis in phrases such as vina, antareṇa, dūre, etc.
- In-depth study of Sati-Saptami and Visheshya-Visheshana relationships.
Unit II - Samaasa:
- Comprehensive understanding of Samaasa and its types.
- Interpretation of the meaning and usage of samasta-padas.
- Determination of the types of Samaasas (Tatpurusha, Dvandva, Bahuvrihi, Avyayibhava).
- Analysis of complex sentences (Dīrgha-vākyeṣu vigrahaḥ).
Unit III - Introduction of Krt and Taddhita Suffixes:
- Familiarization with commonly used krt and taddhita suffixes in Shastras.
- Utilization of dictionaries for interpreting meanings.
- Independent comprehension of dhātu-pāṭha.
- Analysis of notable kṛt-pratyayas and taddhita-pratyayas.
Unit IV - Methodology to Understand Sentences:
- Understanding different types of sentences (vākyāvagama).
- Grasping the meaning of Shastric sentences.
- Application of sentence transformation techniques.
- Introduction to ākāṅkṣā-paddhati and anvaya-krama.
- Establishing the eternal relationship between sentences (yattadornityasambandhaḥ).
- Procedure for determining the intent (tātparya-nirṇayakramaḥ).
Unit V - Balaramayanam – 43 Shlokas:
- In-depth study of Balaramayanam with a focus on 43 selected shlokas.
- Analysis of padavi-bhāga, sandhi, samāsa, and pratyayas in common shlokas.
Self Learning (Lecture Notes), Evaluation & Assessment Methods Used: • Formative Assessment
o Continuous Evaluation (Continuous Assessment)
o Weightage: 100% (Total: 50 marks)
o Pattern: Based on a continuous and comprehensive assessment approach.
o Components: Includes quizzes to evaluate ongoing learning and understanding.
- Summative Assessment
o Final Examination
o Weightage: 100% (Total: 50 marks)
o Format: Comprehension based exam at the end of the course.
o Objective: To evaluate the cumulative knowledge and understanding of the learner regarding the Indic Knowledge tradition and its contemporary relevance.

title: Indian Town Planning and Archit — Overview
content:
Course Name: IKS-V: Indian Town Planning and Architecture
Course Code: SKF-DC-1021
Course credits: 2.0
Learning hours: 20.0
NCrF Credit Level: 5.0
NCrF Credit Points: 10.0
Course Category: Foundation Core
Applicable Areas of Academia: Architecture, Design, Tourism Studies, STEM, Arts & Humanities
L-T-P: 2-0-0
Level: UG
Medium: English
Course Description: The course is intended to provide an overview of India's rich cultural and architectural heritage. It examines how socio-cultural, economic, and environmental factors influenced architectural developments. Through analyzing design principles, temple evolution, and the integration of visual and performing arts in architecture, students will enhance their critical thinking skills, appreciate the legacy of ancient Indian architects, and gain practical knowledge for modern architectural practice.
Intended Objectives: Understanding the interplay among human societies, natural landscapes, and architectural configurations in ancient India.
Developing critical thinking skills by studying socio-cultural, economic, and environmental impacts on architecture.
Appreciating the cultural legacy and inventive methodologies of ancient Indian architects, promoting creativity and sensitivity in contemporary architectural contexts.

Cultivate a deep appreciation for India's cultural and architectural heritage, understanding its significance in shaping contemporary built environments
